name: Luckett procedure

lead: The Luckett procedure is an ear-pinning (otoplasty) technique for prominent ears. A surgeon makes one full-thickness cut in the ear cartilage along the line where the antihelix fold should be, then folds the cartilage so the ear lies closer to the skull.

For appearance, the payoff is ears that no longer stick out from the side of the head, which changes the silhouette of the face from the front. Today it is mostly known as a historical step: its fold could look sharp, and later techniques such as the Converse-Wood-Smith approach were developed to give a softer contour.

paras: It is performed by a surgeon, usually under anesthesia, through an incision behind the ear. Afterwards patients typically wear a dressing and then a snug headband for several weeks while swelling settles, according to general otoplasty descriptions.

Otoplasty in general carries risks of blood collection (hematoma), infection, suture problems and overcorrection that leaves an unnatural contour. The Luckett technique in particular was noted for a fold that looked sharp or unnatural.

angle.text: The procedure changes the shape of the ear cartilage so a prominent ear lies flatter against the head. The result is a permanent surgical change to ear position and fold, rather than something worn or applied.

lead: The Luckett procedure is an otoplasty (ear surgery) technique used to correct prominent ears. It involves a single full-thickness incision through the cartilage along the intended curve of the antihelix, which lets the surgeon fold the antihelix into shape and reduce how far the ear projects from the head.[1]

People who seek ear pinning generally do so to change how their ears look in profile and from the front, and otoplasty is discussed in looksmaxxing circles as a hardmaxxing surgical option for ear prominence. The Luckett approach is mainly of historical interest: its fold was described as sharp and unnatural, and it was later modified into the Converse-Wood-Smith technique, which uses two parallel incisions and tubing sutures for a more natural contour.[1]
infobox: Headband for roughly 3 to 6 weeks (otoplasty generally)

paras: Prominent ears often involve an underdeveloped or absent antihelical fold. Otoplasty techniques are grouped by how they treat the cartilage: some preserve it and reshape with sutures, some cut it so it can be remolded, and some excise portions to reduce projection.[1] The Luckett procedure belongs to the cutting approach: one full-thickness incision follows the desired curve of the antihelix so the antihelix can be folded forward into a fold.[1]

Because the single incision created a fold that could look sharp or artificial, surgeons later moved to the Converse-Wood-Smith method, which uses two parallel incisions and tubing sutures to produce a smoother contour.[1]

Ear reshaping has a long history. Surgery on the ear is described in the Sushruta Samhita (c. 500 AD), Johann Dieffenbach reported an approach for prominent ears in 1845, and Edward Talbott Ely performed an ear pinback in 1881.[1] More than 170 otoplasty procedures have been described.[1]

Surgery in children is commonly done around age 6, when the ear is near adult size, and often under general anesthesia. Operations take roughly 1.5 to 5 hours.[1] A loose dressing is worn for several days, followed by a snug headband for about 3 to 6 weeks; bruising and swelling typically ease within about two weeks.[1]

General otoplasty risks include hematoma, which is drained if it occurs, and infection, which is rare but can progress to perichondritis or chondritis and lasting deformity. Suture extrusion behind the ear is the most common complication and can cause painful granulomas. Overcorrection, producing an unnatural contour, is described as the most significant complication.[1]
